## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_chocolate&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: European encounters")]
On the [fourth voyage of Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_voyage_of_Columbus "Fourth voyage of Columbus"), on 15 August 1502, the expedition came upon a [Mayan trading canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_trade_in_the_Maya_civilization "Maritime trade in the Maya civilization") near an island in the [Gulf of Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Honduras "Gulf of Honduras"). A member of the Columbus expedition, while documenting the items on the canoe, noted the apparent value of cocoa beans based on the canoe crew's reaction when beans were dropped.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013First_Encounter:_Guanaja,_1502-54) However, they did not know what they were, nor that they could be used to make a drink. Spanish conquistador [Hernán Cortés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s "Hernán Cortés") may have been the first European to encounter chocolate when he observed it in the court of [Moctezuma II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moctezuma_II "Moctezuma II") in 1520.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-Dillinger_et_al.-55)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrivetti2008a100-23)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
By 1524, the Spanish had established control over central [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"), and expanded cacao production while increasing tribute requirements[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200415-56) in "frenzied" efforts to profit from cacao.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESampeck201518-57) Cacao was produced using forced labor under the _[encomienda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encomienda "Encomienda")_ labor system. During the 16th century Native Americans experienced a massive [population decline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_the_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas") due to exposure to Eurasian diseases and [direct violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_of_indigenous_peoples "Genocide of indigenous peoples") from colonizers, and production of cacao decreased.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013New_Spain_and_Central_America-58) In response, more cacao was produced on the [Guayaquil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaquil "Guayaquil") coast of Ecuador, as well as in Venezuela, albeit of a lower quality and using slaves from Africa.

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
This cacao was argued to be inferior as it was not the same variety as the Criollo type grown in Mesoamerica: this was the Forastero, which was native to South America and although it yielded more fruit and was more disease resistant, it tasted dry and bitter.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Guayaquil_and_Venezuela-61) As Guayaquil cacao flooded the Mexican market in the early 1600s, dropping prices, Guatemalan [officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Audiencia "Real Audiencia") among others worked to ban Guayaquil cacao from Guatemalan ports and those of [New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain"). Despite bans on importing this cacao around 1630, Guayaquil cacao continued to be exported by smugglers.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPezzarossi2017152-62) The Spanish introduced cacao to the Caribbean around 1525, where it spread from [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad "Trinidad") to [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMomsenRichardson2008a482-63)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
Chocolate was an acquired taste for the Spaniards living in the Americas, widely disliked until the 1590s, and they found the foam particularly objectionable.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022285%E2%80%93288Norton200415-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFew2005677-65) The primarily male Spanish population was exposed to chocolate through the Aztec women they married or took as concubines.

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
As Spanish women immigrated and the Spanish elite ceased marrying local women, Aztec women remained in households as domestic servants.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200415CoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Taste_Barrier-66) Spaniards, [casta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casta "Casta") and Afro-Guatemalan women who couldn't afford domestic servants likely learned to make chocolate from their neighbors.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFew2005677-65) To adapt chocolate to Spanish tastes, it was often sweetened, flavored with familiar spices and served warm,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Taste_BarrierPoelmansSwinnen201614-67) the last change an application of the principles of [humorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humorism "Humorism").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilsonHurst201250-68) The foam was created by just beating the liquid with a _[molinillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molinillo\_(whisk) "Molinillo (whisk)")_ (a wooden whisk) rather than by also pouring it from a height.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Taste_BarrierPoelmansSwinnen201614-67) This habit of serving chocolate spiced to mimic the Mesoamerican flavorings had declined by the 18th century.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200416-69) Women almost always prepared chocolate,

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
and only in rare cases did a man prepare it.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-71)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFew2005678%E2%80%93679-72) During the early colonial period, missionaries sold solid sweet chocolates as delicacies, produced by nuns.
These chocolates were very profitable.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Spain:_%22Chocolate_Brought_to_Perfection%22-73)
[![Image 5: Black and white drawing of three figures in stereotypical ethnic garbs sitting around a table, holding cups](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Cover_of_Philippe_Sylvestre_Dufour_book%2C_17th_century.png/250px-Cover_of_Philippe_Sylvestre_Dufour_book%2C_17th_century.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cover_of_Philippe_Sylvestre_Dufour_book,_17th_century.png)
A 17th-century depiction of a Turk, Chinese, and Aztec drinking coffee, tea, and chocolate. Coffee and tea were introduced to Europe around the same time as chocolate.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English-74)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Still_life_with_a_cup_of_chocolate_by_Spanish_painter_Juan_de_Zurbar%C3%A1n%2C_circa_1640.jpg/250px-Still_life_with_a_cup_of_chocolate_by_Spanish_painter_Juan_de_Zurbar%C3%A1n%2C_circa_1640.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Still_life_with_a_cup_of_chocolate_by_Spanish_painter_Juan_de_Zurbar%C3%A1n,_circa_1640.jpg)
Painting by [Juan de Zurbarán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_de_Zurbar%C3%A1n "Juan de Zurbarán"), depicting the usual way of serving chocolate – from a cup or a bowl, c. 1640

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
The exact date when chocolate was brought to Spain is unknown, and there is no evidence Cortés was responsible for its introduction.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Spain:_%22Chocolate_Brought_to_Perfection%22-73) According to the earliest documented evidence, it was introduced to the Spanish court in 1544 by [Qʼeqchiʼ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q%CA%BCeqchi%CA%BC "Qʼeqchiʼ") Mayan nobles brought to Spain by [Dominican friars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Order "Dominican Order"),[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-Dillinger_et_al.-55) but it was not until 1585 that the first official shipment of cacao to Europe was recorded.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Spain:_%22Chocolate_Brought_to_Perfection%22-73) Through the 16th century, the Spanish were interested in the medicinal qualities of Mesoamerican plants.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Medical_Barrier-75) Writers such as [Bernal Díaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernal_D%C3%ADaz_del_Castillo "Bernal Díaz del Castillo") and [Francisco Hernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_Toledo "Francisco Hernández de Toledo"), the royal physician to [Philip II of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain"),

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
claimed that chocolate was an [aphrodisiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisiac "Aphrodisiac"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAguilar-Moreno2006274-41) and Hernández reported to Spain a range of conditions he believed chocolate and its additives could treat.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Medical_Barrier-75) As a result, Spain during this period viewed chocolate primarily as a medicinal substance.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Spain:_%22Chocolate_Brought_to_Perfection%22-73) By the mid-16th century, chocolate was being manufactured and sold in large quantities.
By the 17th century, Madrid had stored around 700,000 pounds of cacao.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200414%E2%80%9317-76)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
From Spain, chocolate spread to other European nations: to Portugal, to Italy in the 17th century, and then outwards. Religious orders played a significant role in its dissemination.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-77) Tracing the spread of chocolate in Europe is complicated by the religious wars and shifting allegiances of the time, but it is understood that it was driven by [cosmopolitanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitanism "Cosmopolitanism") and missionaries.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200416CoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_Italy:_%22A_More_Exquisite_Gentility%22-78) During the 17th century, drinking chocolate became very popular among the elite of Europe, and was believed to be an aphrodisiac.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English_and_New_Spain_and_Central_America-79) It was expensive due to the high transportation costs and import duties.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGay2008285-80) From the late-16th century until the early 18th century, there was controversy about whether chocolate was both a food and a drink or just a drink; this distinction was important for determining if consumption violated [ecclesiastical fasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasting_and_abstinence_in_the_Catholic_Church "Fasting and abstinence in the Catholic Church").

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
This dispute continued despite popes including [Pope Pius V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Pius_V "Pope Pius V"), [Clement VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VII "Pope Clement VII") and [Benedict XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XIV "Pope Benedict XIV") opining it did not break the fast.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Ecclesiastical_Barrier-81) Most cacao imported to Europe in the 17th–18th centuries came from Venezuela.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Venezuela-82)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
With the difficulty in tracing the spread of chocolate across Europe, it is difficult to pinpoint when chocolate was introduced to France. However, evidence suggests it was first introduced as medicine.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_France-83)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-85) The [silver chocolate pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolatiere "Chocolatiere"), used to stir and beat chocolate, was thereafter invented by the French.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_France-83) By the 1670s, drinking chocolate was widespread among French aristocratic women, despite debate over whether chocolate was medically good or bad, and it would only be settled as beneficial by 1684 with the publication of a thesis defending chocolate by a Paris physician. Concerns about the health effects can be seen expressed in a 1671 letter by noblewoman [Marie de Rabutin-Chantal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_de_Rabutin-Chantal,_marquise_de_S%C3%A9vign%C3%A9 "Marie de Rabutin-Chantal, marquise de Sévigné"): "The Marquise de Coëtlogon took so much chocolate during her pregnancy last year that she produced a small boy as black as the devil, who died."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_France-83)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
Chocolate arrived in England from France around 1657,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESampeck2019107-86) around the same time as tea and coffee, and encountered an initial backlash from those with medical concerns.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English-74)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMomsenRichardson2008b494-87) Cocoa was supplied by Jamaican plantations, after the British [conquered the Spanish territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Jamaica "Invasion of Jamaica") in 1655.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English-74) While chocolate had begun being flavored with new,

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
highly perfumed ingredients such as jasmine and [ambergris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambergris "Ambergris") in Italy in the 17th century,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013143%E2%80%93144-88) in England chocolate was a commercial product and production was simpler and less careful.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English-74) Chocolate was served in coffee houses to whoever could pay,[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacpherson2008322-89) and by the end of the 17th century it was compulsory to include it in [British Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Royal_Navy_(before_1707) "History of the Royal Navy (before 1707)") rations.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins202288%E2%80%9389-90) From England, chocolate spread to the [North American colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_America "British America") by the late-17th century.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English-74) Chocolate was well established among the elite of the late-17th-century Philippines, brought over by the conquering Spanish.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Beyond_Europe-91)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
[![Image 7: Painting of a young woman sitting at a table, pouring chocolate into a cup](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Liotard-Lady_Pouring_Chocolate.jpg/250px-Liotard-Lady_Pouring_Chocolate.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Liotard-Lady_Pouring_Chocolate.jpg)
_A Lady Pouring Chocolate_ by [Jean-Étienne Liotard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-%C3%89tienne_Liotard "Jean-Étienne Liotard") (1744)
In the 18th century, chocolate was considered southern European, aristocratic, and Catholic. This was in contrast to bourgeois coffee and proletarian alcohol. Although the technique of producing chocolate was still very similar to that of Native Americans, chocolate was also consumed as bars, pastilles, in ices, desserts, main courses, and pasta.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chapter_Seven-92) In 1753, Swedish biologist [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") gave cacao its genus name: _Theobroma_, meaning "food of the gods".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chapter_One-93) Medical opinion of this time held that chocolate was medically beneficial if not consumed in excess.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Medical_Experts_Testify-94)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
In Spain, [Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuits "Jesuits") were prominent in importing and drinking chocolate until [Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") expelled them in 1767. The upper and middle class consumed chocolate for breakfast and after dinner, after drinking a glass of cold water. Guilds of chocolate grinders formed across cities.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Spain-95) Recipes featured egg yolks.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarence-Smith200011-96) In Italy chocolate preparation varied.

Source: https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/chocolate_science_history_and_fun_facts_part_1
Title: Chocolate science, history and fun facts – Part 1
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
<dixie@msu.edu>, [Michigan State University Extension](https://www.canr.msu.edu/outreach) - December 23, 2015
Chocolate is a fascinating plant and a fascinating food.
To start this brief serious of articles about chocolate, [Michigan State University Extension](http://www.msue.anr.msu.edu/) will look at its fascinating history and science of this incredible confection called chocolate.
Chocolate beans are the seeds of the cacao tree. Cacao (pronounced ka-KOW) trees grow in the rainforest and the pods grow directly on the trunks of cacao tree. Nearly all cacao trees grow within 20 degrees of the equator and 75 percent of them grow within 8 degrees on either side of it. Cacao originated in Mesoamerica in the Aztec, Olmec and Mayan territories. The Mayans and Aztecs were the first to plant cacao, and have proper claims to being the first cocoa (pronounced KO-ko) farmers, but today most cacao is grown in West Africa. Ghana currently grows the highest quality cocoa beans.
A cacao tree can live over 200 years, but only produces quality cocoa beans for about 25 years. Each year a tree will produce approximately 40 pods. Inside the cacao pods are seeds called cocoa beans. These seeds are the magical ingredient in chocolate.
Cacao trees have blossoms and pods all year long, the white and pink flowers are pollenated by a gnat, who then carries the pollen from one flower to another. It takes about four months for the pod to grow to the size of a small melon and another month to ripen into a yellow to dark orange pod. Each pod contains approximately 40 cocoa beans and is surrounded by a white pulp.
These beans were so valuable to the Aztecs and Mayans that they used them for money, special gifts and offerings to the gods. Taxes of the times could be paid with cocoa beans.
Some fun facts about the value of cocoa beans:
*   200 beans = a male turkey  
*   100 beans = a female turkey or a rabbit  
*   30 beans = a small rabbit  
*   3 beans = turkey egg or an avocado  
*   1 bean = tamale
Money really did grow on trees!

Once the pods are harvested, they are broke open and the beans are scooped out. For the next week, the pods are covered and kept in the dark to ferment. This fermentation process helps to bring out the cocoa’s deep rich flavors. It is reported cocoa beans have more than 300 flavors. After fermenting, the beans are dried in the sun which darken the almond-shaped bean and are shipped to be roasted and processed.
In ancient Mayan civilizations, humans were often sacrificed to guarantee a good cacao harvest. Many tombs dating back more than a thousand years have traces of chocolate. Motechzoma Xocoyotzin (Montezuma ll), the ninth emperor of the Aztecs, was one of the wealthiest men in the world and known as the Chocolate King. At one time he had a stash of nearly a billion cocoa beans. It is no wonder why Swedish scientist Linnaeus named the cacao tree _Theobroma cacao_, meaning “food of the gods.”
Chocolate is one of the oldest natural foods. Up until recent history, chocolate was a bitter drink only enjoyed by the wealthy.
In the next few articles, the history, science and health benefits of chocolate will be examined. Until then, enjoy a few chocolates along with a cup of cocoa. Remember, it’s always a great time to enjoy chocolate!

### **References**
*   [A Brief History of Chocolate](http://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/a-brief-history-of-chocolate-21860917/?no-ist), Smithsonian  
*   [How to Host a Chocolate Tasting Party](http://maketimeforchocolate.blogspot.com/2012/11/how-to-host-chocolate-tasting-party.html), Make Time for Chocolate

[![Image 1: Painting depicting a young woman in a plush bed with a dog on her lap. She is surrounded by three men holding cups.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Ca%27_Rezzonico_-_La_cioccolata_del_mattino_-_Pietro_Longhi.jpg/250px-Ca%27_Rezzonico_-_La_cioccolata_del_mattino_-_Pietro_Longhi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ca'_Rezzonico_-_La_cioccolata_del_mattino_-_Pietro_Longhi.jpg)
_The morning chocolate_ by [Pietro Longhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Longhi "Pietro Longhi"); Venice, 1775–1780
The **history of chocolate** dates back more than 5,000 years, when the [cacao tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theobroma_cacao "Theobroma cacao") was first domesticated in present-day [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador"). Soon after domestication, the tree was introduced to [Mesoamerica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerica "Mesoamerica"), where cacao drinks gained significance as an elite beverage among cultures including the [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_civilization "Maya civilization") and the [Aztecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_Empire "Aztec Empire"). Cacao was considered a gift from the gods and was used as currency, medicine, and in ceremonies. A variety of [cacao-based drinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cacao_beverage "Cacao beverage") existed, including an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting the pulp around the seeds, however, it is unclear when a drink that can strictly be defined as [chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolate "Chocolate") first originated. Early evidence of chocolate consumption dates to 600 BC, when it was often associated with the heart and believed to have [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_drug "Psychedelic drug") properties.
texts.1:
Spanish [conquistadors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistador "Conquistador") encountered cacao in 1519 and brought it to [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), where it was used as a form of medicine. From there, it spread through Europe over the following three centuries, gaining popularity among elites. It was debated for its medicinal and religious merits, and sometimes regarded as an [aphrodisiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisiac "Aphrodisiac"). Following the transformation of chocolate from an elite drink into a solid, widely consumed product due to technological innovations, the 19th century saw the rise of [Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_chocolate "Swiss chocolate") and British chocolate makers, as well as the [industrialization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrialisation "Industrialisation") of production.
Since World War I, chocolate has continued to evolve, leading to the development of [couverture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Couverture_chocolate "Couverture chocolate") and [white chocolate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_chocolate "White chocolate"). Manufacturers have also introduced alternative ingredients such as cheaper fats and [lecithin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecithin "Lecithin"). Production increased dramatically in the 20th century, with new markets emerging in Asia and Africa. Awareness of labor exploitation, especially child labor, has shifted attitudes toward chocolate production. As of 2018, the global chocolate trade was valued at over US$100 billion, concentrated among a relatively small group of cocoa processors and chocolate manufacturers.
texts.2: _Chocolate_ is a Spanish [loanword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loanword "Loanword"), first recorded in English in 1604[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-1) and in Spanish in 1579.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwantonde_%C3%81vilavan_Doesburg2010435-2) Its precise origins are debated.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwanton202423-3) It is popularly thought to derive from the [Nahuatl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahuatl "Nahuatl") word _chocolatl_, as early texts use the term _cacahuatl_ _(_"cacao water") for [cacao drinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cacao_drink "Cacao drink"). Another hypothesis links it to the proposed Nahuatl word _xocoatl_, meaning "bitter drink", though scholars [Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_D._Coe "Michael D. Coe") and [Sophie Coe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Coe "Sophie Coe") argue against this, noting inconsistencies in the phonetic shift from "x" (sh) to "ch".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Language_Barrier-4) A further theory suggests derivation from _chocolatl in a [Mayan language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayan\_languages "Mayan languages"),_ meaning "hot water", though there is no evidence that chocol was used to mean hot.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Language_Barrier-4)
texts.3: Some scholars argue it may come from the [Nawat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawat_language "Nawat language") word _chikola:tl,_[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaufmanJusteson2007193-5) possibly meaning "cacao-beater", in reference to whisking cacao to produce foam. However, the meaning of _chico_ remains uncertain.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaufmanJusteson2007218DakinWichmann200063-6) Anthropologist Kathryn Sampeck suggests that chocolate originally referred to a specific cacao beverage made with [annatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annatto "Annatto") in what is now Guatemala. By about 1580, when the Izalcos were major cacao producers, the word expanded to mean cacao beverages in general.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESampeckThayn201778%E2%80%9379-7)

## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_chocolate&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Cacao domestication in South America")]
The [cacao tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theobroma_cacao "Theobroma cacao") is native to the [Amazon rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_rainforest "Amazon rainforest").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-8) Evidence of cacao [domestication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication "Domestication") exists as early as circa 3300 BC in present-day southeast [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador") by the [Mayo-Chinchipe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayo-Chinchipe "Mayo-Chinchipe") culture, before it was introduced to [Mesoamerica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerica "Mesoamerica").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-9) This emerged from research into residue in ceramics, which revealed [starch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starch "Starch") grains specific to the cacao tree, residue of [theobromine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theobromine "Theobromine") (a compound found in high levels in cacao), and fragments of ancient DNA with sequences unique to the cacao tree.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-11) The domesticated cacao tree was then spread along the [Pacific coast of South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_coast#South_America "Pacific coast").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-12) It is unclear when a drink that could be considered chocolate was first consumed, as opposed to other cacao beverages,

## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
given that there is evidence the [Olmecs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olmecs "Olmecs") fermented the sweet pulp surrounding the seeds into an [alcoholic beverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_beverage "Alcoholic beverage").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Tree_of_the_Food_of_the_GodsCollins2022301%E2%80%93302-13)
texts.7:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Cultivation, consumption, and cultural use of cacao were extensive in Mesoamerica.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacLeod2000636-14) Inhabitants of ancient Mesoamerica created varietals of cacao that grew abundant, high-quality fruit.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESampeckThayn201774-15) The earliest evidence of cacao drink consumption in the region dates to the [Early Formative Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formative_stage "Formative stage") (1900–900 BC). On the [Pacific coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Coast_of_Mexico "Pacific Coast of Mexico") of [Chiapas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiapas "Chiapas"), Mexico, the [Mokayan people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mokaya "Mokaya") consumed bitter frothy watery cacao drinks by 1900 BC. Archaeological evidence from the Gulf Coast of [Veracruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veracruz "Veracruz"), Mexico, demonstrates cacao preparation by pre-Olmec peoples by 1750 BC.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-16) Traces of cacao have been found in bowls and jars dated between 1851 and 1045 BC in the city of [Puerto Escondido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Escondido,_Oaxaca "Puerto Escondido, Oaxaca"), Mexico. The decorations on these ceramics suggest that cocoa was a centerpiece to social gatherings among people of high social status.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdgar201022%E2%80%9323-17)
texts.8:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Although there is evidence that the Olmec consumed cacao as a beverage, little evidence remains on how it was processed. Some evidence suggests cacao consumption in the Olmec regions of [San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Lorenzo_Tenochtitl%C3%A1n "San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán"). Large vases found suggest that the Olmec used cacao for mass gathering events such as sacrificial rituals.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-18)
[![Image 2: A man kneels before a man sitting on a platform. Between them sits a large container.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Mayan_people_and_chocolate.jpg/250px-Mayan_people_and_chocolate.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mayan_people_and_chocolate.jpg)
Image from a [Maya ceramic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_ceramics "Maya ceramics") depicting a container of frothed chocolate
texts.9:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Early evidence for chocolate consumption is found among the [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_civilization "Maya civilization"), in 600 BC.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022298%E2%80%93300-19) Chocolate was used in official ceremonies and religious rituals, at feasts, weddings, and festivals, as funerary offerings and for medicinal purposes.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPresilla200112,_16,_22CoeCoe2013The_Maya_on_the_Eve_of_the_Conquest-20) Both cocoa beans and the vessels and instruments used for preparing and serving chocolate were given as gifts and tributes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPresilla200112,_16,_22-21) It is unknown how, or if, commoners consumed chocolate.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Lords_of_the_Forest:_The_Classic_Maya-22) According to Grivetti (2008), consumption was restricted to adult men, as the stimulating effects were considered unsuitable for women and children.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrivetti2008a100-23) Cocoa beans were also used as a currency by at least 400 BC.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Maya_on_the_Eve_of_the_ConquestLeissle201834-24) Cocoa's social and religious significance motivated rich hobbyist gardeners to cultivate it in [Yucatán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yucat%C3%A1n "Yucatán"), despite the challenging growing conditions.
texts.10:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Nevertheless, most cocoa consumed was imported, primarily from [Chontalpa, Tabasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chontalpa "Chontalpa").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Maya_on_the_Eve_of_the_Conquest-25)
To make chocolate, cacao beans were [fermented](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermentation "Fermentation"), dried and roasted. The Maya then removed the husks and pounded the nibs with _manos_ (stones) on a _[metate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metate "Metate")_ (stone surface) built over a fire, turning them into a paste.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELopez200220-26) This paste was hardened into solid chunks, which were broken up and mixed with water and other ingredients. When heated, a fat called [cocoa butter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocoa_butter "Cocoa butter") rose to the surface and was skimmed off.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELopez200220-26) The basic process of fermenting, roasting, and milling with _metates_ continued unchanged until the 19th century.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELopez200223Presilla200118-27)
texts.11:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Cacao paste was flavored with additives such as [vanilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanilla "Vanilla") and [earflower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cymbopetalum_penduliflorum "Cymbopetalum penduliflorum")[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_Preparation_among_the_Late_Maya-28) (the latter when toasted tasted of [white pepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_pepper "White pepper")).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPresilla2015-29) Before serving, chocolate was poured from a height between vessels to create a highly sought-after brown foam.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Lords_of_the_Forest:_The_Classic_MayaSampeckThayn201777-30) This process also emulsified some cocoa butter that had been added back in.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTELopez200223-31) To assess the quality of the drink, the Maya observed the darkness of the foam, the color of the bubbles and the aroma, as well as the origin of beans and the flavor.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReents-Budet2006215%E2%80%93217-32) Chocolate was only [one of several drinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cacao_beverage "Cacao beverage") made at this time out of cacao, including a drink containing [maize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maize "Maize") and [sapote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapote "Sapote") seeds called _tzune_ and a gruel called _saca_.
texts.12:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
There is uncertainty about how fresh cacao and its pulp were used in drinks.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_Preparation_among_the_Late_Maya-28)
The Maya produced writings about cacao that associated chocolate with the gods, identifying [Ek Chuah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ek_Chuah "Ek Chuah") as the patron god of cacao.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThompson1956545%E2%80%93552CoeCoe2013Twilight_of_the_Classic_Maya-33) There is controversy among historians about whether the mythological figure [Hunahpu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunahpu "Hunahpu") was believed to have invented cacao processing.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013From_Izapan_Civilization_to_the_Classic_Maya-34) Through various eras, cacao was considered a gift from the gods.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVail200810-35) In the late Mayan and during the Aztec periods, there was a strong symbolic connection between cacao and blood.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Lords_of_the_Forest:_The_Classic_Maya-22)
texts.13:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
After the [collapse of the Mayan Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Maya_collapse "Classic Maya collapse"), control over cocoa-producing regions became a source of conflict between the [Toltec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toltec "Toltec") and rival tribes.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPoelmansSwinnen201613-36) Chocolate was consumed as far north as the southern US by the elite of the [Ancestral Puebloans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_Puebloans "Ancestral Puebloans"). During the 9th to 12th centuries, cocoa was imported as part of a cacao-[turquoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turquoise "Turquoise") exchange within a Toltec-run trade network.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Toltecs_and_Beyond-37) The [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_peoples "Maya peoples") introduced chocolate to the Aztecs.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022298%E2%80%93300-19)
[![Image 3: A picture of a woman pouring a liquid from a vessel at a height into another on the floor](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Mujer_vertiendo_chocolate_-_Codex_Tudela.jpg/250px-Mujer_vertiendo_chocolate_-_Codex_Tudela.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mujer_vertiendo_chocolate_-_Codex_Tudela.jpg)
An Aztec woman generating foam by pouring chocolate from one vessel to another in the [Codex Tudela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Tudela "Codex Tudela")
texts.14:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Chocolate was one of the two most important drinks to the Aztecs. It was a luxury, held in particular esteem as the other important drink, _[octli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulque "Pulque")_, was alcoholic, and drunkenness was stigmatized. Chocolate was regarded as a luxurious and sensual product to be celebrated, but at the same time consumption was considered at odds with an imagined austere idealized past, being overly decadent and weakening drinkers.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Attraction_and_Repulsion:_The_Case_of_Octli_and_ChocolateCoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Symbol_and_Ritual-38) It was incorrectly believed to be hallucinogenic. The Aztecs believed cacao was a gift from the god [Quetzalcōātl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalc%C5%8D%C4%81tl "Quetzalcōātl").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022160%E2%80%93162-39) The bean was used as a symbol for the heart removed in human sacrifice, possibly as they were both thought to be repositories of precious liquids—blood and chocolate.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Symbol_and_Ritual-40) The association with blood was reinforced by adding [annatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annatto "Annatto"), a food coloring, to turn the drink red.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022160%E2%80%93162-39)
The Aztecs used chocolate in tributes to rulers and offerings to the gods.
texts.15:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Aguilar-Moreno (2006), citing Colonial Spanish sources, says chocolate was drunk exclusively by the Aztec elites, including the royal house, lords, nobility, and long-distance traders known as [pochteca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pochteca "Pochteca").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAguilar-Moreno2006274-41) At banquets, chocolate was served as a [digestif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ap%C3%A9ritif_and_digestif "Apéritif and digestif") at the end.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Drink_of_the_Elite-42) According to Coe and Coe (2013), soldiers in battle were the only exception to this exclusivity, as chocolate was considered a stimulant.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAguilar-Moreno2006274-41) Chocolate was included in their rations, eaten as pellets or wafers formed from ground cocoa.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Drink_of_the_Elite-42) While [mole poblano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(sauce) "Mole (sauce)"), a sauce that contains chocolate, is commonly associated with the Aztecs, it originated in territory that was never occupied by them,
texts.16:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
and the sauce was only invented after the [Spanish invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Aztec_Empire "Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_Cuisine-43) It was served to human sacrifice victims before their execution.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022160%E2%80%93162-39) Grivetti (2008) says chocolate was also served to the sick, to treat ailments including coughs, stomach issues and fever,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrivetti2008b68-44) and anthropologists [Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carla_Martin_(anthropologist) "Carla Martin (anthropologist)") and Sampeck (2015) say that although chocolate was not consumed in the same way as the elite among commoners during the Postclassical period, it was widely available across Mesoamerica at the time of the conquest for rituals around healing, marriage and travel.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinSampeck201539%E2%80%9340-45)
texts.17:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Cacao was imported into central Aztec territory because frost stopped cacao trees from growing there. Most of the beans came from [Soconusco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soconusco "Soconusco"), a region the Aztecs had conquered specifically for its cacao.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Aztec_%22Chocolate_Tree%22:_Cacahuacuauhuitl-46) The Aztecs required the conquered inhabitants to pay tribute in cacao.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200414-47) At the time of the Spanish conquest, 1.5 million trees were tended in Soconusco. Cacao was transported across Aztec territory by pochteca, carrying 24,000 beans weighing 50–60 pounds (23–27 kg) on their backs.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022160%E2%80%93162-39)
texts.18:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
Although chocolate was primarily served as a drink, it was sometimes eaten.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Attraction_and_Repulsion:_The_Case_of_Octli_and_Chocolate-48) It was served both hot and cold. A gruel made by adding maize was held to be lower-quality than drinks without.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013How_the_Aztecs_Made_ChocolateCollins2022285%E2%80%93288-49) While the highest-quality chocolate was pure, additions were often made, requiring the removal and then replacement of the foam. The most popular addition throughout Mesoamerica was dried and ground chili, though ingredients such as honey, dried and ground vanilla or flowers, and annatto were added.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Flavorings,_Spices,_and_Other_Additions-50) Today, Aztec chocolate drinks are commonly understood to contain cinnamon, despite the spice only being introduced to Mesoamerica by the Spanish conquest.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGanem20203-51) Some Spanish observers claimed that certain chocolate recipes were considered aphrodisiacs, but these reports are not considered reliable.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Flavorings,_Spices,_and_Other_Additions-50) Women were responsible for processing cacao into a beverage.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022160%E2%80%93162-39)
texts.19:
## Early pre-Columbian
### Cacao domestication in South America
The Spanish [conquistadors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistador "Conquistador") recorded the currency value of the cocoa beans, noting in 1545 that thirty beans could buy a small rabbit, one bean could buy a large tomato, and a hundred beans could purchase a turkey hen.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013%22Happie_Money%22-52) Royal stores were claimed to hold massive amounts of cocoa beans.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Royal_Coffers-53) Cocoa beans were often counterfeited, with substitutes including dough made of [amaranth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaranth_grain "Amaranth grain"), wax or broken [avocado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avocado "Avocado") pits.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013%22Happie_Money%22-52)

## Introduction to Europe
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_chocolate&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Introduction to Europe")]
[![Image 4: A painting wherein a Black man kneels on the floor, pushing a cylinder into a slab on the floor. Before him are containers with brown powder, and some formed into brown spheres laid out.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Spanish-Unknown-A-Man-Scraping-Chocolate-69_20_1-739x1024.jpg/250px-Spanish-Unknown-A-Man-Scraping-Chocolate-69_20_1-739x1024.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spanish-Unknown-A-Man-Scraping-Chocolate-69_20_1-739x1024.jpg)

texts.21:
## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_chocolate&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: European encounters")]
On the [fourth voyage of Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_voyage_of_Columbus "Fourth voyage of Columbus"), on 15 August 1502, the expedition came upon a [Mayan trading canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_trade_in_the_Maya_civilization "Maritime trade in the Maya civilization") near an island in the [Gulf of Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Honduras "Gulf of Honduras"). A member of the Columbus expedition, while documenting the items on the canoe, noted the apparent value of cocoa beans based on the canoe crew's reaction when beans were dropped.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013First_Encounter:_Guanaja,_1502-54) However, they did not know what they were, nor that they could be used to make a drink. Spanish conquistador [Hernán Cortés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s "Hernán Cortés") may have been the first European to encounter chocolate when he observed it in the court of [Moctezuma II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moctezuma_II "Moctezuma II") in 1520.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-Dillinger_et_al.-55)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrivetti2008a100-23)

## Introduction to Europe

By 1524, the Spanish had established control over central [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"), and expanded cacao production while increasing tribute requirements[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200415-56) in "frenzied" efforts to profit from cacao.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESampeck201518-57) Cacao was produced using forced labor under the _[encomienda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encomienda "Encomienda")_ labor system. During the 16th century Native Americans experienced a massive [population decline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_the_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas") due to exposure to Eurasian diseases and [direct violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_of_indigenous_peoples "Genocide of indigenous peoples") from colonizers, and production of cacao decreased.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013New_Spain_and_Central_America-58) In response, more cacao was produced on the [Guayaquil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaquil "Guayaquil") coast of Ecuador, as well as in Venezuela, albeit of a lower quality and using slaves from Africa.

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
This cacao was argued to be inferior as it was not the same variety as the Criollo type grown in Mesoamerica: this was the Forastero, which was native to South America and although it yielded more fruit and was more disease resistant, it tasted dry and bitter.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Guayaquil_and_Venezuela-61) As Guayaquil cacao flooded the Mexican market in the early 1600s, dropping prices, Guatemalan [officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Audiencia "Real Audiencia") among others worked to ban Guayaquil cacao from Guatemalan ports and those of [New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain"). Despite bans on importing this cacao around 1630, Guayaquil cacao continued to be exported by smugglers.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPezzarossi2017152-62) The Spanish introduced cacao to the Caribbean around 1525, where it spread from [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad "Trinidad") to [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMomsenRichardson2008a482-63)

Chocolate was an acquired taste for the Spaniards living in the Americas, widely disliked until the 1590s, and they found the foam particularly objectionable.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins2022285%E2%80%93288Norton200415-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFew2005677-65) The primarily male Spanish population was exposed to chocolate through the Aztec women they married or took as concubines.

As Spanish women immigrated and the Spanish elite ceased marrying local women, Aztec women remained in households as domestic servants.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200415CoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Taste_Barrier-66) Spaniards, [casta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casta "Casta") and Afro-Guatemalan women who couldn't afford domestic servants likely learned to make chocolate from their neighbors.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFew2005677-65) To adapt chocolate to Spanish tastes, it was often sweetened, flavored with familiar spices and served warm,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Taste_BarrierPoelmansSwinnen201614-67) the last change an application of the principles of [humorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humorism "Humorism").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilsonHurst201250-68) The foam was created by just beating the liquid with a _[molinillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molinillo\_(whisk) "Molinillo (whisk)")_ (a wooden whisk) rather than by also pouring it from a height.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Taste_BarrierPoelmansSwinnen201614-67) This habit of serving chocolate spiced to mimic the Mesoamerican flavorings had declined by the 18th century.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200416-69) Women almost always prepared chocolate,

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
The exact date when chocolate was brought to Spain is unknown, and there is no evidence Cortés was responsible for its introduction.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Spain:_%22Chocolate_Brought_to_Perfection%22-73) According to the earliest documented evidence, it was introduced to the Spanish court in 1544 by [Qʼeqchiʼ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q%CA%BCeqchi%CA%BC "Qʼeqchiʼ") Mayan nobles brought to Spain by [Dominican friars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Order "Dominican Order"),[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-Dillinger_et_al.-55) but it was not until 1585 that the first official shipment of cacao to Europe was recorded.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Spain:_%22Chocolate_Brought_to_Perfection%22-73) Through the 16th century, the Spanish were interested in the medicinal qualities of Mesoamerican plants.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Medical_Barrier-75) Writers such as [Bernal Díaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernal_D%C3%ADaz_del_Castillo "Bernal Díaz del Castillo") and [Francisco Hernández](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_Toledo "Francisco Hernández de Toledo"), the royal physician to [Philip II of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain"),
texts.29:

claimed that chocolate was an [aphrodisiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisiac "Aphrodisiac"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAguilar-Moreno2006274-41) and Hernández reported to Spain a range of conditions he believed chocolate and its additives could treat.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Crossing_the_Medical_Barrier-75) As a result, Spain during this period viewed chocolate primarily as a medicinal substance.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Cacao_in_Spain:_%22Chocolate_Brought_to_Perfection%22-73) By the mid-16th century, chocolate was being manufactured and sold in large quantities.
By the 17th century, Madrid had stored around 700,000 pounds of cacao.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200414%E2%80%9317-76)

## Introduction to Europe
### European encounters
From Spain, chocolate spread to other European nations: to Portugal, to Italy in the 17th century, and then outwards. Religious orders played a significant role in its dissemination.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-77) Tracing the spread of chocolate in Europe is complicated by the religious wars and shifting allegiances of the time, but it is understood that it was driven by [cosmopolitanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmopolitanism "Cosmopolitanism") and missionaries.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTENorton200416CoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_Italy:_%22A_More_Exquisite_Gentility%22-78) During the 17th century, drinking chocolate became very popular among the elite of Europe, and was believed to be an aphrodisiac.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English_and_New_Spain_and_Central_America-79) It was expensive due to the high transportation costs and import duties.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGay2008285-80) From the late-16th century until the early 18th century, there was controversy about whether chocolate was both a food and a drink or just a drink; this distinction was important for determining if consumption violated [ecclesiastical fasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasting_and_abstinence_in_the_Catholic_Church "Fasting and abstinence in the Catholic Church").

With the difficulty in tracing the spread of chocolate across Europe, it is difficult to pinpoint when chocolate was introduced to France. However, evidence suggests it was first introduced as medicine.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_France-83)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-85) The [silver chocolate pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolatiere "Chocolatiere"), used to stir and beat chocolate, was thereafter invented by the French.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_France-83) By the 1670s, drinking chocolate was widespread among French aristocratic women, despite debate over whether chocolate was medically good or bad, and it would only be settled as beneficial by 1684 with the publication of a thesis defending chocolate by a Paris physician. Concerns about the health effects can be seen expressed in a 1671 letter by noblewoman [Marie de Rabutin-Chantal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_de_Rabutin-Chantal,_marquise_de_S%C3%A9vign%C3%A9 "Marie de Rabutin-Chantal, marquise de Sévigné"): "The Marquise de Coëtlogon took so much chocolate during her pregnancy last year that she produced a small boy as black as the devil, who died."[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_in_France-83)

Chocolate arrived in England from France around 1657,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTESampeck2019107-86) around the same time as tea and coffee, and encountered an initial backlash from those with medical concerns.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English-74)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMomsenRichardson2008b494-87) Cocoa was supplied by Jamaican plantations, after the British [conquered the Spanish territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Jamaica "Invasion of Jamaica") in 1655.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chocolate_and_the_English-74) While chocolate had begun being flavored with new,

In the 18th century, chocolate was considered southern European, aristocratic, and Catholic. This was in contrast to bourgeois coffee and proletarian alcohol. Although the technique of producing chocolate was still very similar to that of Native Americans, chocolate was also consumed as bars, pastilles, in ices, desserts, main courses, and pasta.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chapter_Seven-92) In 1753, Swedish biologist [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") gave cacao its genus name: _Theobroma_, meaning "food of the gods".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Chapter_One-93) Medical opinion of this time held that chocolate was medically beneficial if not consumed in excess.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013The_Medical_Experts_Testify-94)

In Spain, [Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuits "Jesuits") were prominent in importing and drinking chocolate until [Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III_of_Spain "Charles III of Spain") expelled them in 1767. The upper and middle class consumed chocolate for breakfast and after dinner, after drinking a glass of cold water. Guilds of chocolate grinders formed across cities.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoeCoe2013Spain-95) Recipes featured egg yolks.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_chocolate#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarence-Smith200011-96) In Italy chocolate preparation varied.

<dixie@msu.edu>, [Michigan State University Extension](https://www.canr.msu.edu/outreach) - December 23, 2015
Chocolate is a fascinating plant and a fascinating food.
To start this brief serious of articles about chocolate, [Michigan State University Extension](http://www.msue.anr.msu.edu/) will look at its fascinating history and science of this incredible confection called chocolate.
Chocolate beans are the seeds of the cacao tree. Cacao (pronounced ka-KOW) trees grow in the rainforest and the pods grow directly on the trunks of cacao tree. Nearly all cacao trees grow within 20 degrees of the equator and 75 percent of them grow within 8 degrees on either side of it. Cacao originated in Mesoamerica in the Aztec, Olmec and Mayan territories. The Mayans and Aztecs were the first to plant cacao, and have proper claims to being the first cocoa (pronounced KO-ko) farmers, but today most cacao is grown in West Africa. Ghana currently grows the highest quality cocoa beans.
A cacao tree can live over 200 years, but only produces quality cocoa beans for about 25 years. Each year a tree will produce approximately 40 pods. Inside the cacao pods are seeds called cocoa beans. These seeds are the magical ingredient in chocolate.
Cacao trees have blossoms and pods all year long, the white and pink flowers are pollenated by a gnat, who then carries the pollen from one flower to another. It takes about four months for the pod to grow to the size of a small melon and another month to ripen into a yellow to dark orange pod. Each pod contains approximately 40 cocoa beans and is surrounded by a white pulp.
These beans were so valuable to the Aztecs and Mayans that they used them for money, special gifts and offerings to the gods. Taxes of the times could be paid with cocoa beans.
Some fun facts about the value of cocoa beans:
*   200 beans = a male turkey  
*   100 beans = a female turkey or a rabbit  
*   30 beans = a small rabbit  
*   3 beans = turkey egg or an avocado  
*   1 bean = tamale
Money really did grow on trees!
texts.1:
Once the pods are harvested, they are broke open and the beans are scooped out. For the next week, the pods are covered and kept in the dark to ferment. This fermentation process helps to bring out the cocoa’s deep rich flavors. It is reported cocoa beans have more than 300 flavors. After fermenting, the beans are dried in the sun which darken the almond-shaped bean and are shipped to be roasted and processed.
In ancient Mayan civilizations, humans were often sacrificed to guarantee a good cacao harvest. Many tombs dating back more than a thousand years have traces of chocolate. Motechzoma Xocoyotzin (Montezuma ll), the ninth emperor of the Aztecs, was one of the wealthiest men in the world and known as the Chocolate King. At one time he had a stash of nearly a billion cocoa beans. It is no wonder why Swedish scientist Linnaeus named the cacao tree _Theobroma cacao_, meaning “food of the gods.”
Chocolate is one of the oldest natural foods. Up until recent history, chocolate was a bitter drink only enjoyed by the wealthy.
In the next few articles, the history, science and health benefits of chocolate will be examined. Until then, enjoy a few chocolates along with a cup of cocoa. Remember, it’s always a great time to enjoy chocolate!

In 1519 a Spanish soldier named Bernal Diaz walked into the palace of Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlan and watched the most powerful man in the Americas eat dinner. He wrote down everything he saw in extraordinary detail and what he described was unlike anything he had ever encountered in his life.

Over 300 dishes were prepared for Moctezuma every single day. His cooks placed small pottery braziers filled with fire beneath each dish to keep them warm. Turkeys, pheasants, partridges, quails, venison, wild boar, pigeons, hares, and rabbits were among the meats prepared, along with dishes whose ingredients Diaz admitted he could not even identify. Moctezuma would sometimes walk through the kitchen before dining, accompanied by his chefs and stewards, and point at the dishes he wanted, asking what each one was made from before deciding whether to eat it. He was consulted about his own dinner the way a modern head of state is consulted about a policy decision. Over a thousand additional dishes were prepared simultaneously for the guards and attendants waiting outside.

But here is the detail that stayed with Bernal Diaz more than anything else. Moctezuma ate alone, behind a wooden screen, so that no one could watch him. Four women brought his food, presented it on ceramics from Cholula, the finest pottery in the Aztec world. Musicians played. Jesters performed. Acrobats worked in the background. And when the meal was finished, Bernal Diaz wrote in his own words: "from time to time they served him, in cups of pure gold, a certain drink made from cacao." It was said that it gave one power over women, but this I never saw. I did see them bring in more than fifty large pitchers of cacao with froth in it, and he drank some of it, the women serving with great reverence. The golden cup was used once and then reportedly thrown into the lake alongside the palace. Moctezuma did not drink from the same cup twice.

That chocolate was nothing like what you know today. No sugar, no milk, no sweetness. Pure cacao ground and mixed with chili, vanilla, and water, beaten until it frothed, served cold or at room temperature, and reserved almost entirely for the ruler, the nobility, and warriors being rewarded for battlefield valor. A source from the period describes the restriction in terms that left no ambiguity: if one of the common people drank it without sanction, it would cost their life. Cacao beans were currency, ranked alongside gold and gems in records of solemn offerings to the dead, and the idea that a commoner might casually consume a cup of it was treated the same way a medieval peasant drinking from the king's personal chalice would have been treated. While Moctezuma finished his fifty pitchers of frothy gold cup chocolate, the farmers and laborers who grew the cacao he was drinking ate two meals a day. Maize porridge with chili in the morning. Tortillas, beans, and squash in the afternoon. On a good day there were grasshoppers roasted with salt and lime, or dried lake algae pressed into a cake that the Spanish described as tasting faintly like cheese. The distance between those two tables, in the same city, on the same evening, was one of the widest gaps between imperial and commoner food in the entire ancient world.

Tenochtitlan was built on an island in the middle of a lake with almost no natural farmland surrounding it, and feeding a city of 200,000 people required a food supply system of extraordinary sophistication. The floating garden fields called chinampas, anchored in the shallow lake bed, produced up to seven harvests a year and fed the city through a network of canals that brought produce directly from the fields into the market at Tlatelolco. Bernal Diaz walked through that market as well and wrote that he had never seen anything like it in his life, that it was larger than any market in Rome or Constantinople, and that he could not find the words in Spanish to describe the quantity and variety of what was for sale. He was a man who had traveled extensively across the known world and he stood in the middle of an Aztec market in 1519 and admitted it was beyond his vocabulary.

Moctezuma was executed by the Spanish in 1520 and the city of Tenochtitlan was razed and rebuilt as Mexico City in 1521. The golden cups went to the bottom of the lake and the wooden screen came down and the 300 dishes were never prepared again. But the market at Tlatelolco is still there, and Mexico City is still built on the same island, and the descendants of those commoner farmers are still eating tortillas, beans, and chili on the same ground where all of this happened.
